text: Connecting a host to a local MCP server is configuration, not code you write as the agent builder. Claude Desktop reads a JSON config file -- a set path on macOS, another on Windows -- listing each server's name and how to launch it.

When Claude Desktop starts, it reads that file, launches each configured server as a local process, and creates one MCP client per server -- exactly Lesson 13's one-client-per-server rule. The official Filesystem Server is a real example: once configured, Claude Desktop gains tools for reading, creating, and searching files, with every action still requiring your explicit approval.

Once a client connects, it doesn't already know what the server offers -- it asks. That's the discovery handshake: the client calls tools/list, and resources/list if relevant, and gets back the server's full set of definitions. From the host's perspective, those tools now simply exist, ready to offer the model exactly like a hand-written Chapter 2 tool.

This doesn't change the agent loop from Lesson 2 -- Plan, Act, Observe stays the loop. What changes is where the Act step's tools come from: before, your own code defined them; now, they can be discovered at connection time from a server someone else built.

Connect to two servers and you get two separate client connections, each with its own discovered tools -- but from the model's point of view at the Act step, it's just one combined pool to choose from, the same tool-selection problem Lesson 9 already covers. Next: when to reach for MCP versus building a tool yourself.
